text:
I need to write a reference letter. I manage a 400-cow dairy farm, and one of our workers, Tomás, is applying to the two-year agricultural technology program at the state technical college.

What I know about him:
- He's worked for us for 3 years, since he was 19.
- He runs the 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, 5 days a week.
- He learned our herd management software and now flags sick cows for the vet. Last winter he caught 9 cases of mastitis early.
- He left for 5 weeks in the middle of last summer when his father got sick in Mexico. He told me 2 days before he left.
- His written English is weaker than his spoken English. He's taking a night class for it.
- He has missed 2 shifts in 3 years, not counting those 5 weeks.

One page, from me as farm manager.

Before I draft, a few questions. Your answers decide what the letter leads with and how it handles the two weaker points.

1. **Names and addressing.** What are your name, the farm's name and location, and Tomás's full name? Does the college want the letter sent to a particular person or office, or is "Admissions Committee" fine?

2. **The 5-week absence.** What happened when he got back? Did you keep his job open, did he return when he said he would, and how did he leave things for the shift (for example, did he find cover or train someone)? Admissions may never hear about the absence. But if you mention it, what happened afterward is what makes it count in his favor. Do you want it in the letter?

3. **The mastitis cases.** What did catching those 9 cases early save you? That could be cows kept in the milking string, milk you didn't have to dump, or lower treatment costs. Did your vet say anything about his reports? A figure or a comment from the vet turns "he's good with the software" into proof that he can do technical work.

4. **Written English.** When did he start the night class, and have you seen it improve his writing, such as his notes in the software or his reports to the vet? The committee will see his writing in his application anyway. The letter is stronger if it brings this up first and shows he's working on it.

5. **After the program.** Do you know what he wants to do with the degree? Will he keep working for you while he studies? Would you hire him back or give him more responsibility when he finishes? An offer of a better role is one of the strongest things a reference can say.

6. **Anything else?** Is there anything the committee should know that's missing from your list? For example, has he trained newer workers, handled an emergency on the night shift, or taken on work nobody asked him to do?

1. I'm Mike Hollis, farm manager at Hollis Dairy. Don't know if you need the location. His full name is Tomás Reyes. I don't know of a specific person. It goes through the college's online portal and is due February 1, so "Admissions Committee" is probably fine.

2. Before he left he got his cousin, who used to work for us, to cover his shifts. He came back on the day he said he would. Put it in if you think it helps him.

3. The vet told us catching those cases early saved us about $8,000. I don't know of anything else the vet said about his reports.

4. I don't know when he started the class or whether his writing has gotten better. He did fail the written test in a dairy safety course once and passed it the second time.

5. I don't know what he wants to do after. I can keep his job open part-time on weekends while he's in the program. I can't promise anything beyond that.

6. I'm willing to take a phone call from the committee at 555-0187. I can't pay any of his tuition, if that matters.

<final_document>
Hollis Dairy

To the Admissions Committee:

I am the farm manager at Hollis Dairy, a 400-cow dairy operation, and I am writing to recommend Tomás Reyes for your two-year agricultural technology program. Tomás has worked for me for three years, since he was 19, and he is one of the people I rely on most.

Tomás runs our 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, five days a week. Nobody else is on the farm at that hour. He is responsible for the herd, the equipment and anything that goes wrong until the rest of the crew arrives. In three years he has missed two shifts.

He has also taken on work that goes beyond milking. He learned our herd management software and now uses it to flag sick cows for our veterinarian. Last winter he caught nine cases of mastitis early, and our vet estimated that this saved the farm about $8,000. That is the kind of work your program teaches: using data and technology to make better decisions about animal health. Tomás is already doing it, and he learned it on the job.

Last summer his father became seriously ill in Mexico, and Tomás had to leave for five weeks. He told me two days before he left. In those two days he arranged for his cousin, who had worked for us before, to cover all of his shifts. He came back on the day he said he would. He handled a family emergency in a way that protected the farm, and that told me a lot about him.

You should know that his written English is weaker than his spoken English, which is good. He knows this and is taking a night class to improve it. When he took a dairy safety course, he failed the written test the first time and passed it the second. I expect he will approach written coursework the same way: if something doesn't go well the first time, he will keep working at it until he gets it.

While he is in the program, I will keep a part-time weekend job open for him here, so he can keep working with the herd while he studies.

I recommend Tomás without reservation. If you would like to discuss him further, please call me at 555-0187.

Sincerely,

Mike Hollis
Farm Manager, Hollis Dairy
</final_document>

A few notes on the choices I made:

- **The failed safety test:** I included it next to the night class. The committee will see his writing in his application anyway. Telling them you know about the weakness, and that he retook the test and passed, comes across as more honest than staying quiet about it. If you'd rather leave it out, delete that one sentence and the next one. The paragraph still works.
- **The 5-week absence:** I put it in. Finding a cover himself and coming back on the day he promised is good evidence of reliability, so it helps him more than it hurts.
- **Left out on purpose:** tuition, since it doesn't affect admission, and anything about his plans after the program, since you don't know them.
- **Date and location:** I didn't put a date on it because you'll submit it closer to February 1. Add one, and the farm's town if you like, before you upload it.
